beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The hard part is not access; it is absorption.
beats.got: Buying licences doesn't mean people use the thing. I've seen that with three programmes.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: I have an example, the ERP reporting module nobody opened. No prework otherwise.

beats.trigger: **Interview** for your teammate's job-to-be-done using the agentic Jobs-to-be-Done pattern (Clayton Christensen and collaborators), and write the outcome statement as the design contract
beats.got: A list of verbs and no figure. 'Absorb' and 'propagation' are consultant words.

beats.trigger: Two questions to warm up: who's the one person who came to mind just now? And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: I'm supposed to hand something to a person. I haven't built any agent system in Modules 2-6, so this assumes work I haven't done. 'What makes you hesitate' is a feelings question.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from the colleague's task, not from the tool. That is reasonable. 25 minutes with no cost attached.

beats.trigger: If it could describe anyone in the room, point to the generic line and ask the agent to try that part again.
beats.got: Check whether the output is specific. That is a test I can apply, but I'd use it on my own material, and nobody asked for my spreadsheet.

beats.trigger: *"Share the whole agent"* is a vendor pitch and is NOT on the list.
beats.got: Four ways to share, and the one the vendors sell is excluded. I like that it says so up front.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: A plan in 23 minutes. Still no cost or payback.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: One root obstacle instead of a list of twelve. That is how I'd read a risk register.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: Missing owners show up as a finding, the same way I'd catch a budget with no budget owner. That is a risk named before I raise it.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plan is a hypothesis, not a promise. Fair.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: What would have to be true for them to switch. That's a business-case question I recognise, although nobody puts a figure on it here.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem. Imagine it failed and write why. I recognise this as proper risk work.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Picking a tool because it fits the platform is shopping. That is what we did with the last software purchase.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Speed and quality alone means it went shallow.
beats.got: The goal should be something beyond faster and better, like a dependency removed. Still no figure.

beats.trigger: Hand someone the agent file and you have handed them the shell of a thing whose contents are still on your disk and in your head.
beats.got: The value sits in the person's accumulated corrections, not in the tool. So it is not a licence you hand over.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Someone has to answer for what the thing does, and that part can't be bought. A CFO understands that.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Rollout metrics count seats, not use. Every programme I've seen reported seats. This is the point that matters to me.

beats.trigger: Michael Polanyi, a philosopher of science, had the line for it: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: A philosopher quote. I take it that people need something familiar to hang the new thing on.

beats.trigger: In the full agent picture, this is the interface piece.
beats.got: I haven't seen the full picture from the earlier modules. All I take is that other people's calendars matter.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: Fifteen people, two workshop days, a proposal, and no decision because urgency moved on. I recognise it from the board, and it is a first-person account, not a US case.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The alternative is the current spreadsheet or gut call, not 'do nothing'. That is a baseline I can price.

beats.trigger: Whether they pick it up is their decision, made for their own reasons, on a Tuesday you will not be in the room for.
beats.got: You can't force adoption. Fine, but a bit poetic.

beats.trigger: A missing name is a finding: it marks the part of this that is not built yet
beats.got: If you can't put a name on who owns it, it isn't ready. I use the same test on budget lines.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent summarises and I push back. A step I've not done, so I skim.

beats.trigger: Save the conversation. It's the bridge to when work resumes.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Access is easy; absorption is scarce.
beats.got: Four short lines I can repeat to the CEO.

beats.trigger: Test one assumption. Ask for one name. Talk to one person.

take_homes: Rolling out access is not the same as people using it. Seats are not use, and the report should say which one it is.
If nobody has a name on who answers for it, it isn't ready. I'll use that as a test for any proposal that lands on my desk.
Ask what the person does today before offering the tool. The alternative is the spreadsheet or gut call they already have, and it has to be beaten on something checkable.

monday.move: Ask my controller how the month-end variance commentary gets written today, who writes it, how long it takes, and what they'd need to see to trust a draft from an agent. I'll write down the answers and won't build anything yet.
monday.when: Monday, 15 minutes after the morning meeting
monday.stop_condition: If she can't give me hours and a figure for the current process, I drop it, because there's nothing to measure against.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, so even if the answers are good I can't test anything on real numbers.

misconception.why: I came in thinking AI is a licence you buy. The point that access is a switch and absorption happens in other people's weeks, together with the story of the 2026 value-stream project, makes me think it is something the organisation has to build. I'm not fully convinced, because no cost or payback figure was given.

one_line: Good on why rollouts fail and who owns what, but I got no number I could take to the board, and I'd have liked to see the cost per month before the philosophy.
